title: Glass Bottle Supply for Spirits | Craft Beer School
desc: How spirit bottles are made, why glass furnaces shape supply and lead times, the common Indian sizes and the defects buyers check for.
teaser: The bottle often costs more than the whisky inside a regular brand. Here is how glass supply works and why it runs on long lead times.
standfirst: Every bottle of whisky starts in a furnace that never switches off. For buyers, planners and marketers in spirits companies, this guide explains how glass bottles are made, what drives cost and lead time and what to check before a delivery reaches the bottling line.
sections: Glass is made in furnaces that run for years

Spirit bottles are usually soda-lime glass, made by melting sand, soda ash and limestone with crushed recycled glass, called cullet. The furnace runs at around 1,500 °C. Once lit, a glass furnace is kept running continuously for many years, because cooling and reheating it damages the lining. A full rebuild is a major project.

That one fact shapes the whole supply chain. A glassworks wants its furnaces full all the time. It schedules production in long runs of each bottle design and colour. Changing colour in a furnace takes time and wastes glass. Buyers who understand this get better prices and more reliable deliveries.
From gob to bottle in seconds

Molten glass flows out of the furnace and is cut into gobs, each one the weight of a single bottle. Forming machines with several sections drop each gob into a blank mould, blow or press it into a rough shape, then transfer it to a finishing mould where it is blown to final shape. The bottles then pass through a long oven called a lehr, which cools them slowly so the glass does not crack under internal stress.

The moulds are the part buyers pay for directly. A standard bottle shape uses moulds the glassworks already owns. A custom shape, embossed logo or unusual base needs new moulds. That adds cost and a lead time of several months before the first bottle is made.
Colour, weight and size drive the price

• Colour. Clear flint glass is the most common for whisky because it shows the colour of the spirit. Extra flint, a clearer grade with fewer impurities, costs more and suits premium brands. Green and amber are used for some spirits.
  • Weight. Heavier bottles with thick bases look premium but use more glass and energy and cost more to ship.
  • Size. In India, 750 ml, 375 ml and 180 ml are the workhorse sizes for spirits. Smaller packs make up a large share of bottles in the regular tier, which means more glass per litre of whisky sold.
  • Shape. Standard round bottles run fastest on both the glass line and the bottling line. Unusual shapes slow both.
Energy and soda ash move the cost

Glass making uses a great deal of energy, usually natural gas or other fuel to heat the furnace. When fuel prices rise, glass prices follow, often with a lag written into supply contracts. Soda ash is another major input. Using more cullet lowers the furnace temperature needed and the energy used, which is why glassworks value good supplies of clean, sorted broken glass.

For a spirits company, this means glass price changes are often predictable months in advance if someone is watching fuel and soda ash prices. Our guide to whisky packaging cost drivers puts glass in context with the other components.
Planning lead times around the festive peak

Glass is bulky, fragile and expensive to store. Glassworks usually make each design in campaigns and ship to a schedule. Spirits demand in India peaks in the festive season, so bottle demand peaks in the months before it, along with every other producer's.

Planners who wait until the last moment compete for the same furnace time and transport. Agreeing annual volumes with suppliers, sharing forecasts early and holding a sensible safety stock of bottles before the peak all help. For state-specific packs, remember that glass embossed for one market cannot always be used in another.

Glass is recyclable without loss of quality. Higher recycled content also lowers furnace energy. In India, used spirits bottles are also collected and traded. Some bottles go back into circulation. That has an uncomfortable side. An empty bottle of a known brand is valuable to anyone selling spurious liquor.

Brands respond with features that make refilling harder or easier to spot: non-refillable closures, embossed glass, holograms and serialised codes. Several states also require their own security labels. Each of these adds cost and planning steps. For the buyer, it means glass and closure decisions are also brand protection decisions. A cheaper, generic bottle may be easier for a counterfeiter to copy. A distinctive one costs more but carries a measure of protection.
What to check before glass reaches the line

Quality teams inspect incoming glass by sampling each delivery against an agreed standard. Common defects include stones (unmelted particles), seeds and blisters (bubbles), checks (small cracks), thin walls and finishes that are out of shape. The floor detail that matters most is the finish, the top of the neck where the closure sits. A finish a fraction of a millimetre out can cause leaks, loose caps or bottles that jam the capper.

A broken bottle on a high speed filling line can stop production and contaminate neighbouring bottles with glass fragments, so lines have procedures for glass breakage. Our guide to designing a premium whisky bottle covers the brand side of glass choices. A good first step for a buyer is to walk the bottling line with the quality team for one shift and note every stoppage caused by glass.
faqs: Why does custom glass take so long?
A new shape or embossing needs new moulds, which take months to make. The glassworks then has to fit the run into its furnace schedule.
Clear glass, the most common choice for whisky because it shows the spirit's colour. Extra flint is a clearer, more premium grade.
What bottle sizes are common for spirits in India?
750 ml, 375 ml and 180 ml are the most common, with other sizes used by some brands and states.
